newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH SDP CRITICISES GOVT SOCIAL SECURITY REPORT.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH SDP CRITICISES GOVT SOCIAL SECURITY REPORT.

text.p: The parliamentary group of Finland's Social Democratic Party (SDP) -- the biggest group in parliament and government -- on Tuesday criticised a government report on social security.
The government said new social security expenditure cuts may be necessary to live up to the criteria for EMU unless economic growth developed in line with forecasts.
"This ominousness is repeated several times in the report. The hint is worrying, even outright threatening," MP Marjatta Vehkaoja told parliament, speaking on behalf of the SDP group.
The legislature's debate on the report started on Tuesday.

Vehkaoja said many experts were of the opinion that next year, "income differences will rise strongly unless unemployment falls" following the five-party left-right-green government's 1997 budget decisions to lower income taxes and cut social security.

MP Annika Lapintie, speaking on behalf of the parliamentary group of another coalition party, the Leftist Alliance, said the report showed that "unfortunately the government wants to close its eyes to the dangerously increasing divides in society".
The unemployed were becoming disillusioned. This was evident from the low turnout in the October 20 elections, she said.
"Especially in all cities of any size, voting proved least interesting in areas with the highest rates of unemployment," Lapintie said.
She called for social policy measures to prevent people from being left permanently outside the mainstream of society and condemned the emergence in Finland of "cold right-wing values".
Sounding a different note, MP Irja Tulonen of the Conservative Party -- also a coalition partner -- said the government should cut income taxes further to boost the incentive to seek employment.
"It is clear that all achieved benefits cannot be retained," Tulonen said.

And MP Pehr Lov of the Swedish People's Party -- a junior coalition partner -- said the report was flawed in its assertion that Finland was well placed to meet the social security challenges of the future thanks to a system with tripartite talks between the government, trade unions and employers.
"This entire concept reflects the belief that welfare can be distributed already before it has been created," Lov said.
Economic growth and lower unemployment required adjustment to new types of jobs and lower labour costs, he said.
